subject: English
description: Coordinating, subordinating, correlative, conjunctive adverbs; error detection and fill-in-the-blank

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She was tired, ___ she continued working.'
questions.explanation: 'Yet' (a coordinating conjunction) expresses contrast — she was tired BUT still continued. 'So' would mean the tiredness caused her to stop. 'For' introduces a reason (= because). 'Or' introduces an alternative.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He will pass ___ he studies hard.'
questions.explanation: 'If' sets a positive condition — passing depends on studying. 'Unless' = 'if not', meaning he will pass only if he does NOT study, which is the opposite meaning. 'Although' = despite. 'Since' introduces a reason or elapsed time.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She was ill, ___ she did not go to school.'
questions.explanation: 'So' indicates result/consequence — being ill caused her not to go. 'But' and 'yet' both signal contrast (she was ill BUT went), which contradicts the sentence. 'Or' introduces an alternative.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: '___ you leave now, you will miss the train.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless' = 'if not'. The sentence means: if you do NOT leave now, you will miss the train. 'If you leave now' would mean leaving causes you to miss it — the opposite logic. 'Although' = despite. 'Because' = reason.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He is poor ___ honest.'
questions.explanation: 'But' signals contrast between two seemingly contradictory qualities. Being poor and being honest are presented as an unexpected combination. 'And' would just add two qualities without any contrasting nuance.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'We stayed indoors ___ it was raining.'
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason/cause for staying indoors. 'Although' would imply they stayed despite the rain (contradicts the natural response). 'Unless' = 'if not'. 'Until' relates to time.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Wait here ___ I come back.'
questions.explanation: 'Until' marks the end-point of an action — wait and keep waiting up to the point I return. 'Since' marks a starting point in the past. 'When' marks a single moment, not a duration. 'While' indicates simultaneous actions.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He is neither honest ___ hard-working.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' is a correlative conjunction pair that negates both elements. 'Neither...or' is grammatically incorrect. 'Neither...and' is not a recognized correlative pair. The correct correlative is always 'neither...nor'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Not only did she sing, ___ she also danced.'
questions.explanation: 'Not only...but (also)' is a fixed correlative conjunction pair. The second clause amplifies the first. 'And' does not form a correlative pair with 'not only'. Note the inversion: 'Not only DID she sing' (auxiliary verb moves front).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Either Rahul ___ Priya will attend the meeting.'
questions.explanation: 'Either...or' is the standard correlative pair presenting two alternatives. 'Either...nor' is incorrect (nor pairs only with neither). 'Either...and' is not a valid correlative pair.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'I will wait ___ you arrive.'
questions.explanation: 'Until' marks the endpoint of the waiting — the waiting stops when you arrive. 'Since' (as a time conjunction) refers to a past starting point. 'For' is a preposition/conjunction of reason. 'While' indicates simultaneity, not endpoint.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He ran fast ___ missed the bus.'
questions.explanation: 'Yet' (or 'but') signals a contrast — despite running fast, he still missed the bus. This is an unexpected outcome. 'So' would imply running fast caused him to miss the bus, which is the opposite. 'Because' introduces a reason.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Both my sister ___ I will attend the function.'
questions.explanation: 'Both...and' is the correct correlative pair that joins two subjects inclusively. 'Both...or' and 'Both...nor' are not valid correlative pairs. 'And' here makes both subjects attend — the only valid completion of 'both'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'I will go ___ you come or not.'
questions.explanation: 'Whether...or not' expresses that the action holds in both scenarios — regardless of whether you come. 'If' sets only one condition (you come → I go), not both. 'Whether' is always used when two alternatives cover all cases.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: '___ he is rich, he is not happy.'
questions.explanation: 'Although' (= though/even though) introduces a concessive clause — something true but unexpected given what follows. Being rich yet unhappy is a contrast. 'Because' would imply richness causes unhappiness. 'Therefore' and 'So' indicate consequence.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'No sooner had he entered the room ___ the lights went out.'
questions.explanation: 'No sooner...than' is a fixed correlative adverbial. 'No sooner...when' is a common error — the correct pair is always 'than'. Note: 'No sooner' triggers subject-auxiliary inversion in formal writing: 'No sooner HAD he entered...'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Neither the manager nor the employees was present at the meeting.'
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. 'Employees' (plural) is the nearer subject, so the verb must be 'were present', not 'was present'. This is the proximity rule for correlative conjunctions.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Hardly had she finished her work ___ the boss called.'
questions.explanation: 'Hardly/Scarcely/Barely...when' is the correct fixed pattern. 'No sooner...than' uses 'than', but 'hardly/scarcely/barely' always pairs with 'when'. Mixing them ('hardly...than') is a common exam trap.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses conjunctions correctly?

options.option_text: Although he tried, but he failed.
Despite he tried hard, he failed.
In spite of he tried, he failed.

questions.explanation: 'Although...but' is redundant — both signal contrast. Use one or the other: 'Although he tried, he failed' OR 'He tried but failed'. Options C and D are wrong because 'despite' and 'in spite of' are prepositions that must be followed by a noun/gerund, not a clause: 'Despite trying hard' / 'In spite of his effort'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She is not only beautiful ___ also intelligent.'
questions.explanation: 'Not only...but (also)' is the fixed correlative pair. 'Not only...and' is not a standard correlative. 'But also' completes the pair by amplifying the first quality with an additional one.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Both the principal as well as the teachers were present.'
questions.explanation: 'Both' must pair with 'and': 'Both the principal AND the teachers'. Using 'as well as' with 'both' is non-standard. 'As well as' is correct only when used independently: 'The principal as well as the teachers was/were present' (no 'both').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She would rather read books ___ watch TV.'
questions.explanation: 'Rather than' is a fixed prepositional phrase used for comparison or preference. 'Then' is an adverb of time/sequence, not a comparative conjunction. The pattern is: 'would rather [action A] than [action B]'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Scarcely had the match begun ___ it started raining.'
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely...when' is the correct pair. A key exam rule: 'hardly/scarcely/barely' → pair with 'when'; 'no sooner' → pair with 'than'. Mixing these is the most tested conjunction error in SSC/banking exams.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank (conjunctive adverb): 'I was very tired; ___, I finished the assignment.'
questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless' is a conjunctive adverb meaning 'in spite of that' — it signals contrast after a semicolon. 'So' would be a coordinating conjunction (no semicolon structure). 'Although' needs a clause, not a semicolon. 'Nevertheless/However/Nonetheless' all work here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The weather was bad; ___, we decided to go out.'
questions.explanation: 'However' (conjunctive adverb) signals contrast after a semicolon. 'So' and 'therefore' both mean 'as a result', which would mean bad weather caused them to go out — illogical. 'Because' introduces a cause, not a contrast.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'I worked very hard ___ I could support my family.'
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces a purpose/result clause — the hard work was done with the aim of supporting the family. 'Because' would mean supporting the family caused the hard work (reverse logic). 'So that' answers 'why?' with an intended outcome.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Both Ravi and Raj has completed the project successfully.'
questions.explanation: 'Both...and' always creates a plural compound subject, requiring a plural verb. 'Has completed' (singular) must be 'have completed'. Unlike 'either/or' and 'neither/nor' (proximity rule), 'both...and' invariably takes a plural verb.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'I will take this job ___ the salary is low.'
questions.explanation: 'Even though' (stronger than 'although') marks a concession — accepting the job despite the acknowledged obstacle of low salary. 'Because' would mean the low salary motivates acceptance. 'Unless' means 'if not', reversing the logic.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He arrived late; ___ he missed the introduction.'
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' (conjunctive adverb) signals a result/consequence after a semicolon — arriving late caused missing the introduction. 'Although' would imply he missed it despite arriving on time. 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction that connects clauses differently (no semicolon structure).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Neither he nor she are coming to the function.'
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject. 'She' is singular, so the verb must be 'is coming', not 'are coming'. Proximity rule: the verb takes the number of the subject immediately before it.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The task is difficult; ___, it is not impossible.'
questions.explanation: 'However' (conjunctive adverb) signals contrast between two independent clauses joined by a semicolon. The second clause qualifies the first. 'And' and 'also' add information without contrast. 'So' signals consequence.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Not only ___ she pass the exam, but she also topped the batch.'
questions.explanation: When 'not only' begins a sentence or clause, subject-auxiliary inversion is required in formal English: 'Not only DID she pass...' The auxiliary 'did' (simple past) inverts with the subject. Using 'she did' (normal order) is incorrect after fronted 'not only'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He behaves ___ he were the owner of the company.'
questions.explanation: 'As if' (= as though) introduces a hypothetical/unreal comparison and is followed by the subjunctive 'were' (not 'was'). 'Like' is a preposition in formal English — not a conjunction (avoid 'like he were...'). 'As' alone does not introduce a hypothetical clause.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He had no sooner landed at the airport ___ reporters surrounded him.'
questions.explanation: 'No sooner...than' is the only correct pairing. 'No sooner...when' is incorrect, even though 'barely/hardly/scarcely' use 'when'. This is the key distinction tested repeatedly in competitive exams.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

options.option_text: Although he was tired, but he continued working.
Despite being tired, he continued working.
In spite of he was tired, he continued working.
Though he was tired, but he continued working.

questions.explanation: Option B uses 'despite' correctly (preposition + gerund 'being tired'). Options A and D have the 'although/though...but' redundancy error. Option C misuses 'in spite of' before a full clause; it needs a noun or gerund: 'in spite of his tiredness' or 'in spite of being tired'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'He left early lest he might be late for the meeting.'
questions.explanation: 'Lest' is a formal conjunction meaning 'for fear that'. It must be followed by 'should', not 'might' or 'would': 'lest he should be late'. Using 'might' with 'lest' is incorrect. The correct sentence: 'He left early lest he should be late.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Such was his dedication ___ he never missed a single day of practice.'
questions.explanation: 'Such...that' is the correlative pair for degree/result. Here 'Such' is already in the sentence; the blank needs 'that'. The pattern: 'Such was his [noun] that [result clause]'. Compare: 'So + adjective/adverb + that' vs 'Such + (a) + noun + that'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The harder you work, ___ better your results will be.'
questions.explanation: 'The + comparative...the + comparative' is a fixed parallel construction expressing proportional relationship. 'The harder...the better' — both parts need 'the'. This is not an article but a conjunction-like correlative structure in English grammar.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'I was so exhausted ___ I could hardly keep my eyes open.'
questions.explanation: 'So...that' is the correlative expressing degree and result — the exhaustion was so extreme that the stated consequence followed. 'So + adjective/adverb + that + result clause'. Compare: 'Such + (a/an) + noun + that...'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The sooner you start, ___ better your chances of success.'
questions.explanation: The comparative correlative 'the...the' requires 'the' before each comparative adjective/adverb: 'The sooner...the better'. This structure expresses a direct proportional relationship between two actions.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'The moment when he saw her, he was instantly reminded of his sister.'
questions.explanation: 'The moment' already functions as a conjunction/time expression, making 'when' redundant. The correct form is 'The moment he saw her...' Similarly, 'the day', 'the minute', 'the instant' all directly precede the clause without 'when'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Provided ___ you submit the application today, the scholarship will be processed.'
questions.explanation: 'Provided that' (= 'on the condition that') is the standard formal conditional conjunction. While 'if' is synonymous, 'provided' must always be followed by 'that' in formal usage. 'Provided if' is incorrect — it is never used.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Barely had the award ceremony ended ___ the power went out.'
questions.explanation: 'Barely' belongs to the 'hardly/scarcely/barely' group, which always pairs with 'when', never 'than'. The inverted structure is: 'Barely had [subject] [past participle] when [past simple clause]'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'No sooner...than' correctly?

options.option_text: No sooner she arrived than the party began.
No sooner had she arrived than the party began.
No sooner she had arrived when the party began.
No sooner had she arrived when the party began.

questions.explanation: Option B is correct: inversion (had + subject) after 'no sooner' + 'than'. Option A lacks inversion. Option C has wrong pairing (when instead of than) and no inversion. Option D has inversion but wrong conjunction (when). Both inversion AND 'than' are required.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'He is so weak that he cannot hardly walk without support.'
questions.explanation: 'Cannot hardly' creates an illogical double negative (cannot + hardly both carry negative force). The correct forms are: 'can hardly walk' OR 'cannot walk without support'. Mixing 'cannot' and 'hardly' together is a standard error tested in competitive exams.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank — complete the correlative pair: '___ was his arrogance ___ everyone in the room avoided him.'
questions.explanation: 'Such + noun + that' expresses degree. 'Arrogance' is a noun, so 'such...that' is correct. 'So...that' uses an adjective or adverb: 'He was SO arrogant THAT...' With a noun ('arrogance') the correct structure shifts to 'Such was his arrogance THAT...'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'He went to the office in spite of he was seriously ill.'

options.option_text: in spite of he was seriously ill

questions.explanation: 'In spite of' is a preposition and must be followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. Correct: 'in spite of being seriously ill' OR 'in spite of his serious illness'. Alternatively, replace with the conjunction 'although/even though': 'although he was seriously ill'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: 'As though' is a conjunction equivalent in meaning to which of the following?
questions.explanation: 'As if' and 'as though' are interchangeable — both introduce a hypothetical or unreal comparison, typically followed by subjunctive mood: 'He speaks as if/as though he were an expert.' They both mean 'in a manner suggesting that [something unreal is true]'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'No sooner had the alarm rung ___ he was wide awake.'
questions.explanation: 'No sooner...than' — the invariable rule: 'no sooner' takes 'than', period. This is distinct from 'hardly/scarcely/barely' which take 'when'. Both patterns require subject-auxiliary inversion: 'No sooner HAD the alarm rung THAN...'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Scarcely he had entered the hall when the applause began.'
questions.explanation: Negative adverbs like 'scarcely', 'hardly', 'barely', 'no sooner' placed at the start of a clause require subject-auxiliary inversion. Correct: 'Scarcely HAD HE entered the hall when...' The normal subject-verb order 'he had' must be inverted to 'had he'.
questions.subject: English
